gemma4_verdict: Gemma 4 31B (dense, served bitsandbytes int4 in the Labmate spec; GGUF Q4_K_M / MLX also available) is a strong generalist coder driven heavily by its thinking mode. Google reports LiveCodeBench v6 80.0%, Codeforces ELO ~2,150 (up 20x from Gemma 3 27B's 110), AIME 2026 89.2%, GPQA Diamond 84.3%, MMLU-Pro 85.2%, BigBench Extra Hard 74.4%, and a dramatic agentic-tool-use jump (tau2-bench Retail 86.4% vs Gemma 3's 6.6%). It has native function calling and is multimodal (text+image, variable aspect ratio, plus document parsing), which is unique among the two for reading paper figures/charts. No official isolated HumanEval or DS-1000 (scientific-Python) number was published; LiveCodeBench v6 80.0% and CF ELO 2,150 are the strongest available coding proxies and exceed Qwen3-32B's LiveCodeBench (~65-70 thinking). However, Gemma 4 is a generalist, not a code-specialized model: it was not trained on the 5.5T code-token corpus that the Qwen Coder line was, and its real-world agentic repo-editing (SWE-bench Verified) lead is reported as weaker than dedicated coder models. Practical caveat: the vLLM gemma4 tool-call parser has active bugs (pad-token corruption under concurrent tool-call requests requiring a serialization lock; reasoning_content not populated because special channel tokens are stripped; reports of broken tool calls under Claude Code / OpenCode), which is directly relevant to Labmate's MCP tool-calling loop. [uncertain]
qwen3_verdict: Qwen3-32B (dense, Apache 2.0, 128K context, GGUF/AWQ widely available) is a general-purpose reasoning model rather than a code specialist. Official/aggregated numbers: LiveCodeBench it wins versus Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct; thinking-mode LiveCodeBench is roughly 65-70 (the 32B sibling in the technical report's ablation reaches ~60 on LCBv5 at the 8B-scale study, with the 32B higher), AIME 2024 81.4%, Arena Hard 93.8%, LiveBench 74.9%, MMLU-Pro (base) 65.5%. On real agentic SWE work it is weak: SambaNova measured only 15.2% on a 100-sample SWE-bench Verified subset with mini-SWE-agent (vs DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.3%, and the dedicated Qwen3-Coder ~69.6% on the full set). It has strong tool-calling (uses the standard hermes parser in vLLM, mature OpenAI-format fidelity) and benefits from being newer than Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. For scientific Python it inherits Qwen's strong code-data lineage but the base 32B is text-only (no figure reading). The community view (r/LocalLLaMA) is that Qwen2.5-Coder-32B is now 'outdated' and Qwen3 models are preferred for coding, but for serious agentic coding the dedicated Qwen3-Coder variant, not Qwen3-32B, is recommended. [uncertain]
benchmarks: LiveCodeBench: Gemma 4 31B 80.0% (v6) vs Qwen3-32B ~65-70 (thinking, LCBv5-class) [uncertain]. HumanEval: no official Gemma 4 31B figure; Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct 92.7% (Qwen3-32B not separately reported, expected high-80s/low-90s) [uncertain]. SWE-bench Verified (agentic): Qwen3-32B 15.2% (100-sample subset, mini-SWE-agent); Gemma 4 31B not officially published, reported to trail dedicated coder models; dedicated Qwen3-Coder ~69.6% for reference. Codeforces ELO: Gemma 4 31B ~2,150 vs Qwen3 flagship 2,056 [uncertain for 32B]. MMLU-Pro: Gemma 4 31B 85.2% vs Qwen3-32B-base 65.5%. GPQA Diamond: Gemma 4 31B 84.3% vs Qwen3-32B mid-60s [uncertain]. AIME 2024/2026: Gemma 4 31B 89.2% (AIME 2026) vs Qwen3-32B 81.4% (AIME 2024). Scientific-Python (DS-1000 / SciCode / DSCodeBench): neither model has published numbers; DS-1000 (numpy/pandas/matplotlib/scipy/sklearn/pytorch/tf) and SciCode are the right benchmarks but were not run on either model in public sources [uncertain].
factual_accuracy: No code-specific hallucination eval was found for either model. As a coding-relevance proxy, Gemma 4 31B's much higher GPQA Diamond (84.3% vs Qwen3-32B mid-60s) and MMLU-Pro (85.2% vs 65.5%) suggest stronger grounded scientific knowledge, which reduces confabulation when implementing domain algorithms. For library-API correctness (avoiding hallucinated numpy/pandas/torch APIs, i.e. slopsquatting-style errors), no DS-1000-style API-constraint pass rates were published for either model. [uncertain]
inference_speed: No direct non-CUDA tok/s benchmark for either 31B/32B model at Q4/Q5 with llama.cpp or MLX was found in sources. Both are similar-size dense models (31B vs 32B) so raw throughput at equal quant should be comparable; expect roughly 15-35 tok/s on an M3/M4 Max (32-64GB) class machine for a ~31B dense model at Q4. Gemma 4's hybrid local/global sliding-window attention reduces KV-cache memory and aids long-context speed. Gemma 4 31B's heavy thinking-mode (4,000+ reasoning tokens) increases wall-clock latency per answer despite per-token speed, which matters for Labmate's interactive agentic loop. No MTP/speculative-decoding advantage was confirmed for either. [uncertain]
multimodal_support: Gemma 4 31B: image (and document-parsing) input with variable aspect ratio/resolution and a configurable visual-token budget (70/140/280/560/1120 tokens per image); smaller Gemma 4 variants also add audio/video. This lets it read paper figures, training-curve plots, and architecture diagrams directly. Qwen3-32B: text-only; the multimodal capability lives in the separate Qwen3-VL line, not the 32B dense base. For ML-experiment work (reading a loss/accuracy curve screenshot, a figure from a paper), Gemma 4 31B is the only option of the two.
context_window: Gemma 4 31B: 256K nominal, with credible RULER recall reported as competitive with hosted frontier models (effective usable context well into the high tens/low hundreds of K) [uncertain on exact RULER number]. Qwen3-32B: 128K nominal; effective long-context recall not separately measured in sources [uncertain]. For coding/ML work both comfortably hold a full paper (8-20K) and large code context; Gemma 4's 256K is the better fit for whole-repo or multi-file experiment context plus a paper in the same window.
non_cuda_support: Both ship GGUF (llama.cpp: ROCm via -DGGML_HIPBLAS=ON / HIP, Vulkan, and Metal) and Qwen3-32B additionally has wide AWQ/GPTQ coverage; Gemma 4 31B has official GGUF + MLX (Unsloth, Ollama gemma4:31b including q4_K_M, nvfp4, and an explicit mlx tag; LM Studio). Gemma 4 31B needs ~20GB at 4-bit / ~34GB at 8-bit, so it fits a single 32GB non-CUDA GPU (AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX 24GB is tight at 4-bit, W7800 32GB comfortable) or Apple Silicon M3 Max / M4 Pro with 32-64GB unified memory (runs comfortably). Qwen3-32B 4-bit has a similar ~20GB footprint and the same hardware applies. Build complexity is standard llama.cpp/MLX for both; Gemma 4 has the smoother MLX/Ollama day-one story, Qwen3 the broader quant-format ecosystem. [uncertain on exact AMD model validation]
over_refusal_risk: No XSTest or coding-specific refusal data was found for either model in this research pass. Generally, code-generation and ML-experiment requests are low-sensitivity, so over-refusal is unlikely to obstruct Labmate's coding tasks for either model. Dual-use/security-research coding (e.g. exploit or malware-adjacent code) could trigger refusals on both; no comparative numbers available. [uncertain]
ecosystem_toolchain: Both have day-one llama.cpp/GGUF, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, and Unsloth support; Gemma 4 31B additionally has strong MLX coverage. Key difference for tool-calling: Qwen3-32B uses vLLM's mature hermes parser with well-tested OpenAI tool-call fidelity, whereas Gemma 4 31B requires --tool-call-parser gemma4 (a custom non-JSON serialization) plus --reasoning-parser gemma4 and a specific chat template, and that path currently has open vLLM bugs (pad-token corruption under concurrent tool calls needing a serialization lock; reasoning_content stripped; reports of broken tool calls in Claude Code/OpenCode). This is directly load-bearing for Labmate's MCP JSON-RPC tool loop and is the strongest argument for Qwen3 on the agentic surface. HuggingFace model cards and quantized availability are good for both.
labmate_relevance: HIGH. Coding ML experiments (PyTorch/JAX pipelines, training-curve analysis, implementing paper methods) is one of Labmate's four core functions, and the spec explicitly provisions a Qwen2.5-Coder-32B specialist worker. This dimension directly decides whether Labmate needs a separate coding worker at all and which model fills each role.
recommendation: On pure coding/ML capability for Labmate, Gemma 4 31B is the stronger single model: it beats Qwen3-32B on LiveCodeBench (80.0 vs ~65-70), Codeforces ELO, GPQA, MMLU-Pro and AIME, and is multimodal (can read training-curve plots and paper figures Qwen3-32B cannot). For sub-question (3): Qwen3-32B does NOT clearly beat Gemma 4 31B at coding, so there is no case for Qwen3-32B replacing BOTH the orchestrator and the coding specialist on capability grounds. The realistic architecture choices are: (a) Use Gemma 4 31B as both orchestrator AND coding worker IF the vLLM gemma4 tool-call/reasoning-parser bugs are resolved or worked around (serialization lock) — this collapses the two roles and Gemma 4's higher coding scores justify it; (b) Keep the Labmate spec's split but consider upgrading the coding worker from Qwen2.5-Coder-32B (now community-considered outdated) to a dedicated Qwen3-Coder variant (~69.6% SWE-bench Verified) for real agentic repo-editing, since both Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3-32B are weak on SWE-bench-style multi-file agentic edits. The decision tipper: if Labmate's coding tasks are mostly single-file synthesis, paper-to-code, and curve analysis (its actual use case), Gemma 4 31B alone suffices and removes a model; if it grows into autonomous multi-file repo editing, add a dedicated Qwen3-Coder worker rather than relying on Qwen3-32B. Note SWE-bench/HumanEval/DS-1000 numbers for Gemma 4 31B are unpublished, so pilot both on Labmate's own ML-coding tasks before committing.
